page.title: PerformanceDaddy — See what is slowing your Mac
page.description: Inspect Mac background apps, processes, listening ports and RAM. PerformanceDaddy records slowdown evidence and reviews targets before stopping work.

hero.title:
A slow Mac.
*A clearer picture.*
hero.lede: See what is running behind the scenes on your Mac. Inspect background apps and helpers, find the process holding a port, watch RAM and local coding agents, and record evidence while a slowdown is happening.
hero.note: Public early-access beta · free to download · macOS 14+

header.title: Find it. Inspect it. *Decide.*
header.lede: Move from the symptom you can see to the process and resource evidence behind it. Stopping a process always starts with a review.

items.title: Find who *owns the port.*
items.body: Search listeners by port number or process. Sort CPU and RAM, inspect process duration and recognized local agent families, then review exact targets before a normal or force stop. No remote port scanning or cloud agent sessions.

detail.alt: Port search for 5000 returning ControlCenter as the owning process, with its resident RAM

items.title: Record *the slow moment.*
items.body: Capture CPU work, memory headroom, active swap-out, thermal state and disk capacity for 15 seconds or two minutes. Every run gets an evidence assessment and a next check, including when the measured signals cannot explain the delay.

detail.alt: Diagnostic recording setup with a 15-second or two-minute length and the measured domains: CPU, memory and swap, thermal state, disk headroom

blocks.eyebrow: Start with what you can measure
blocks.title: A busy process is a clue. *It is not the whole story.*
blocks.lede: A port can be occupied while CPU is quiet. Allocated swap does not prove active paging. PerformanceDaddy puts the observations, their limits and the next check together.

blocks.title: Your work is *not the payload.*
blocks.lede: Process inspection does not collect command arguments, environment variables or agent conversations. Configuration inventory reads bounded file metadata, not contents. A separate terminal experiment runs your startup scripts only after explicit consent.

blocks.title: For a Mac full of *moving parts.*
blocks.lede: The public beta is a signed and notarized universal build for macOS 14 or later, free during early access. A diagnostic report distinguishes measured signals from a confirmed cause; it cannot explain every slowdown.

points.title: Made for
points.body: Developers running local servers and coding agents who want visible ports, understandable processes, RAM evidence and deliberate stop controls.

points.title: Not for
points.body: Automatic optimization, cloud-session monitoring, remote network scanning, fan control or a promise to identify every root cause.

Yes, after review. Normal and force stops are separate choices, guarded by process identity and user restrictions. Stopping a process can interrupt work or lose unsaved data.

items.q: What about apps running in the background?
items.a: Inspect visible background processes and app helpers alongside foreground workloads. Compare their CPU and resident RAM, see how long a process has been running, and inspect available identity and startup metadata before deciding what to stop. Background does not mean unnecessary: macOS and your apps rely on many of these helpers.

items.q: Why did something come back after I stopped it?
items.a: An app, login item or service manager may launch another process. PerformanceDaddy shows matching launch-configuration clues and watches for matching executables after stops requested through the app. A match is not proof of an automatic restart or its cause. This history stays in memory for up to 24 hours and clears when you quit; the app does not disable startup items for you.
Local metadata recognition covers Codex, Claude, Devin, Hermes, Aider, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and Cursor CLI. It cannot identify every wrapped launch or tell whether a conversation is active.

items.q: Does every report prove the root cause?
items.a: No. Reports separate observed signals, thresholds not met and missing evidence. CPU activity is not proof of why a task was slow. Network latency, blocked threads, GPU activity and disk latency are not measured by the standard recording.

items.q: Can it read fan speed or temperature?
items.a: The app reports macOS thermal state and available power evidence. Raw fan RPM, temperature and fan controls are not implemented.
